top_choice_rationale: P001 (Helpman and Melitz, B044) is the best-bounded achievement on the slate. Melitz (2003) is a single originating model that moved trade analysis from the industry to the firm and made selection and within-industry reallocation central to the gains from trade. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus foreign direct investment is a separable extension. The qualitative predictions have been tested in firm-level data for over twenty years, and the disputes concern welfare magnitudes, not whether the mechanism exists. The 2008 prize covered earlier increasing-returns trade theory, so I treat it as adjacency, not duplication. The main weakness is attribution: Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum are outside a two-name award. I would word the citation around the theory of selection and the gains from trade, and I would not claim welfare magnitudes. P002 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) is a serious and mature body of work, ranked second. Its credit boundary is unstable: it may be two strands, and a three-name cap excludes Dorn. The task framework also has priority claims outside the ballot, and China-shock persistence is still debated. I rank P002 above no award because it is a substantial achievement that could be cited honestly if worded around the empirical evidence. My own preferred part from the opening, B037 (Kiyotaki and Moore), is not on the slate and so cannot be ranked. The support count is not evidence of merit.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for Helpman, Melitz, Autor, Hanson or Katz. I am an IIES colleague and frequent co-author of committee members Krusell and Boppart, and I co-authored a menu-cost paper with Friberg, but none of these papers concerns a candidate on the slate. The 2018 Scientific Background cites my own 2014 climate paper, which is not a shortlisted candidate. Conflicts are disclosed but not adjudicated.
